title: Balaji Vishwanath Writes a New State

title_i18n.en: Balaji Vishwanath Writes a New State

subtitle: From Konkan Accountant to Architect of the Maratha State
era: Rise of the hereditary Peshwa, 1713-1720 CE
moral: Institutions can outlast the victories that create them.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar, Balaji Vishwanath letters and early Shahu-period documents
sources.note: Primary Modi-script administrative evidence for the early Peshwa system.

sources.citation: Khafi Khan, Muntakhabu-l-Lubab, account of the Syed Brothers and Delhi politics
sources.note: Persian narrative context for the 1719 Mughal settlement.

sources.citation: Andre Wink, Land and Sovereignty in India (Cambridge UP, 1986)
sources.note: Key interpretation of chauth, sardeshmukhi and Maratha sovereignty claims.

panels.shot: low-angle mid-shot with distant Mughal Delhi skyline on one side and the forts of the Deccan on the other

dialogue.text: In the troubled years after Aurangzeb, Balaji Vishwanath Bhat rose from Konkan accounts to write a new Maratha state into the very ledgers of empire.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of the Konkan coast and a modest village house

dialogue.text: He was not born into a fort or a war camp. Balaji Vishwanath learned his craft among ledgers, rains and salt air along the Konkan coast.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up of Balaji writing accounts

dialogue.text: Around him, Maratha power was still a patchwork of forts and chiefs. In his hands, scattered dues and promises began to take the shape of a system.

panels.shot: medium shot in a Maratha military camp tent, papers spread out

dialogue.text: He moved from village books to camp chanceries, where silver, grain and horse fodder mattered as much as courage. He learned how a kingdom eats, marches and pays.

panels.shot: wide shot of Satara palace hall with Shahu on a distant throne and Balaji in the foreground

dialogue.text: By the time Shahu claimed his grandfather’s mantle, the Maratha court was a field of rival claims. Balaji brought not banners, but order to Shahu’s fragile throne.

panels.shot: close, dignified mid-shot of Balaji receiving a ceremonial robe in court

dialogue.text: In 1713, Shahu made him Peshwa. It was more than a title. It meant the pen that balanced war and revenue would now sit in one patient Konkan hand.

panels.shot: bird's-eye shot of the Deccan with overlaid suggestion of routes and revenue circuits

dialogue.text: The Marathas already claimed chauth and sardeshmukhi across the six Deccan provinces. But these dues were won by raids and memory. Balaji sought to turn them into recognized rights.

panels.shot: medium shot of Balaji at a low desk with Modi-script letters and seals

dialogue.text: In the Peshwa daftar, he stitched scattered pattis, sanads and promises into a fiscal constitution: which village owed what, to whom, and under whose seal.

panels.shot: wide shot of Satara court with nobles debating, Balaji listening

dialogue.text: Meanwhile in Delhi, emperors were made and unmade by favourites. News of the Syed Brothers’ rise reached Satara. Shahu’s men argued: fight, raid, or bargain?

panels.shot: low-angle close-up of Balaji’s face, lit by lamp, thoughtful

dialogue.text: Balaji saw a different road: help decide who sat on the Mughal throne, and in return, make the empire itself write the Maratha claims into law.

panels.shot: wide shot of a Maratha column marching north across the plains

dialogue.text: In 1719, he went north with Maratha strength at his back. Not as a conqueror of Delhi, but as an arbiter in its civil war.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of Mughal Delhi skyline and Red Fort

dialogue.text: Delhi still glittered, but its marble hid fractures. The Syed Brothers needed allies. Balaji offered soldiers and pressure, not submission.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot in a Mughal tent, Balaji seated across from a Persian noble

dialogue.text: In the language of khilats and farmans, he pressed his case: Maratha support for the Syeds’ emperor, in return for written recognition of chauth and sardeshmukhi in the Deccan.

panels.shot: close-up of imperial hand signing a farman, Balaji’s hand steadying the page

dialogue.text: The farmans that followed named the six Deccan provinces and granted Marathas the right to collect their shares. Raids became revenues; assertion became recognized sovereignty.

panels.shot: medium shot in a Mughal courtyard, Yesubai being escorted out as Balaji watches

dialogue.text: Another clause released Shahu’s mother, Yesubai, from Mughal prison. The settlement was not only about silver; it was about honour and the memory of Shivaji’s house.

panels.shot: wide shot of Satara court welcoming Balaji’s return, with documents presented to Shahu

dialogue.speaker: balaji_vishwanath_bhat
dialogue.text: Maharaj, the empire itself has written our rights. Now we must keep them.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of Balaji instructing younger officials in the daftar

dialogue.text: He then did the slower work: folding imperial grants into Maratha registers, training men who could read both Persian and Modi, binding distant villages to Satara through ink.

panels.shot: medium shot of Balaji in Pune, overlooking warehouses and markets

dialogue.text: Power began to tilt from the old hill capital to Pune, where revenues, records and officers could be managed like a great machine. The Peshwa’s seat was becoming the real centre.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of Balaji with his son Bajirao by lamplight

dialogue.text: When illness bent his body, he prepared his son Bajirao to inherit not just an office, but a structure: armies funded by regular dues, chiefs bound by shares in a wider Maratha commonwealth.

panels.shot: solemn close-up of Balaji resting, eyes closed, with records beside him

dialogue.text: Balaji Vishwanath died in 1720, the same year Bajirao was made Peshwa. His office had quietly become hereditary, turning a royal advisor into the pivot of a confederacy.

panels.shot: broad, contemplative aerial shot of the Deccan and north India with faint traces of Maratha routes and forts

dialogue.text: Battles would be won and lost, and dynasties would rise and fall. But the fiscal-military frame Balaji forged—of chauth, sardeshmukhi and a Peshwa’s statecraft—outlived the victories that first made it possible.
